summary:
We built ByteMe, an interactive Earth System Trend Detective. Users can ask a question like “Is Svalbard losing snow?”, select a region on the map, and explore 52 NASA measurements spanning land, oceans, ice, and the atmosphere. ByteMe charts monthly records, accounts for seasonal cycles, and shows how fast a measurement is changing and whether the trend is statistically significant.

Our Trend Decomposer helps users investigate what might be driving that change. They choose possible drivers, see how much of the observed trend each can statistically account for, and test whether those relationships hold up when the records are shifted out of sync. The app also shows how much of the trend remains unexplained. We built ByteMe to make NASA data accessible to students and give them practice weighing evidence before drawing conclusions about cause and effect.
details:
Find out what is changing. ByteMe combines live NASA POWER records with prepared NASA satellite and model grids. Users can search in everyday language, click the world map, or investigate an area such as a country or the Amazon. The app plots monthly observations, estimates a season-adjusted linear trend, and reports the rate per decade, a 95% confidence interval, and a plain-language verdict. Users can change the time window and see how the result compares with the full record. They can also find distant places where several measurements are changing in a similar pattern.

Test a possible explanation. Our creative contribution is the Trend Decomposer. Suppose snow depth and air temperature both change over decades. To test whether they move together on shorter timescales, ByteMe first removes the seasonal patterns and long-term trends, then checks whether unusually warm months also tend to have unusually shallow snow. It fits several candidate drivers together and uses the fitted relationships to estimate how much of the long-term trend each statistically accounts for. A chart shows the contributions, their uncertainty, and the trend that remains.

Try to weaken your own explanation. ByteMe runs an “alibi check” that shifts a candidate driver’s record by whole years and repeats the analysis. If misaligned records give similarly strong results, the original timing offers weaker evidence. Users can also check whether the pattern appears at similar latitudes and try another NASA data product where one is available. In our Svalbard example, the fitted temperature contribution was about 0.4 cm per decade out of an observed snow-depth decline of about 4.8 cm per decade. Its uncertainty range included zero, and most of the decline remained unexplained by the selected drivers. Students can see both why warming is worth investigating and how much uncertainty remains about its role.

Build for students using real data. We built the site with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using MapLibre for maps and Plotly for charts. We used Python to prepare NASA grids and develop the reference trend calculations. Search combines keyword rules with a sentence model that runs in the browser to match questions by meaning. We designed around missing months, differences in coverage, and the fact that consecutive observations can be related. Our goal is for a student to leave with a finding they can explain: what changed, how much it changed, which possible drivers they checked, and what the data still leave open.
dataRefs: NASA POWER – Monthly Weather and Solar Data
NASA GLDAS Noah – Monthly Soil Moisture, Evaporation, and Runoff
NASA Terra MODIS – Monthly Vegetation Greenness (NDVI)
NASA Terra MODIS – Monthly Land Surface Temperature
NASA Aura OMI – Tropospheric Nitrogen Dioxide
NASA Aqua AIRS – Monthly Surface Air Temperature
NASA Giovanni – Earth Science Time Series Explorer
